title: Transaction
text:
The neon housing above the Redmond quick-mart shivered against the corrugated sheet metal every time the sulfur wind came off the Barrens, a rhythmic metallic rattle in the damp cold. Inside, heat radiated off the rusted coils of an automated soykaf brewer behind the scratched laminate counter, competing with the sour green glow of a pirated local grid terminal looping reruns of old Neo-Tokyo urban combat trids. Lee Ji-yoo set three certified credsticks on the counter beside a small paper sack of synthetic strawberry drops. The clerk’s dented cyber-optic whirred, its autofocus hunting for a clean lock across the shadowed bridge of her nose, caught by the suffocating, motionless symmetry beneath the grease-stained canvas.
“Need a bag?” the clerk asked, his voice rasping through an artificial vocal box scarred by industrial soot.
“No,” she said. The voice was Lee Ji-yoo’s, soft, clear, and quiet, though the resetting cartilage in her throat still radiated a dull, grinding ache from the shift thirty minutes prior. The bone-latch behind her jaw throbbed with residual metabolic heat, holding the narrowed zygomatics in place while her dermal weave adjusted to the cold wind. She kept the oversized collar of the heavy oilskin coat pulled high, burying a jawline smoothed of any native human imperfection. The clerk’s cyber-optic whirred, its autofocus hunting for a clean lock across the shadowed bridge of her nose, caught by the suffocating, motionless symmetry beneath the grease-stained canvas. She slid the paper sack into her pocket, took a single wrapped hard candy, and stepped out onto the wet gravel beneath the rattling eave.
The wrapper tore with a brittle pop. She slipped the pink sugar sphere past her teeth, muscles in her jaw working against the stiff tension of the cosmetic shift. The chemical strawberry flavor hit her tongue with a sharp, synthetic coldness that left an oily film over her enamel.
Jin-Young had been five years old when that specific coldness first touched his palate, arriving on the same rain-drenched morning as the talent suit from Mitsuhama. The man had stepped out of an armored black sedan into the grey Manila humidity, wearing a three-piece suit of dust-repelling charcoal weave that shed the mud of the Tondo floodway without a stain. He had walked through the narrow alley where the sewer ditches overflowed with brackish tide water, his polished calfskin boots stepping deliberately across the cinder blocks to avoid the spots where raw drainage pooled against the wooden shanties.
Inside the shack, the torrential monsoon rain drummed against the rusted tin roof with the steady force of thrown gravel. Jin-Young’s father sat on the edge of the wood-frame cot with his hands wedged tight between his knees, staring down at knuckles scarred from thirty years of shipyard welding along the Pasig canal. His mother stood by the single kerosene burner, where a dented aluminum pot of thin rice gruel simmered with bitter melon greens, her fingers twisting the frayed hem of her faded cotton shirt until the seams pulled taut against her knuckles.
The suit stood in the center of the dirt-floor room, completely dry, bringing with him the smell of sterile corporate air conditioning and expensive fabric protectant. His sensor specs threw thin green diagnostic reticles across Jin-Young’s face, measuring the distance between the boy’s temples and the precise curvature of his nasal cartilage. His gaze ignored the water pooling in the corner and the damp laundry hanging from the ceiling rafters, focusing entirely on the biological geometry before him.
“The expression is clean,” the suit said, his voice carrying the flat, measured detachment of a customs inspector checking freight manifests. His gloved fingers hooked beneath Jin-Young’s chin with unhurried pressure, dry leather pinching tender skin as he tilted the boy’s head toward the grey daylight leaking through the open doorway. His thumb pressed the hinge of the jawbone, gauging the spacing of the facial cartilage and the solid obsidian depth of the Dalakitnon iris against the light. “The subterranean variance has settled properly in the bone structure. The vessel is clean. The baseline deviation fits the primary export profile, and we will claim the biological deduction under Section Twelve.”
“He’s quiet,” his mother whispered, her eyes locked onto the floor near the clay water jar where Jin-Young sat watching the silver thread on the suit’s cuffs. “He doesn’t cry. Even when the fever came last winter, he stayed quiet.”
The suit tapped the edge of a silver datapad with a manicured fingernail, checking the genetic telemetry feeds. “Compliance is factored into the initial grading matrix. The vocal geometry shows early resonance markers. The shaping spells will take cleanly to the cartilage before the pubertal growth cycle sets the bone.” He spoke with the same dry cadence vendors at the corner palengke used when weighing scrap iron on a hanging scale.
The man reached into his breast pocket and laid a heavy silver credstick on the rough wooden table.
“Ten thousand nuyen,” the suit said, the silver plastic gleaming bright and sterile against the stained grain of the wood. “Certified by Mitsuhama Financial Services. The remainder of the stipend will be held in corporate trust, payable upon completion of the secondary reconstruction cycle in Kyoto.”
The shack was completely silent except for the roar of the rain on the tin roof and the steady drip of water falling into an empty tin can behind the cot. Jin-Young’s father kept his eyes locked on his calloused hands, motionless on the rough mattress. His mother’s hand hovered above the table for two long seconds, her fingers trembling against the humid air before they closed around the cold silver casing, tucking it deep into her apron pocket.
“Gather his things,” the suit said.
“He has no things,” his father said, his voice dropping into the dirt floor between his feet.
The neighborhood children stood along the mud alley in the pouring rain, watching in silence as the suit led Jin-Young toward the waiting sedan. The car’s windows were dark smoked glass with the triple-rhombus crest of Mitsuhama etched into the corner. The driver opened the rear door, releasing a blast of refrigerated, dust-filtered air that made Jin-Young shiver through his thin cotton shirt.
The door sealed with a heavy pneumatic thud, cutting off the sound of the rain and the smell of the slum in an instant. Through the dark glass, Jin-Young watched his mother standing in the doorway of the shack, her right hand pressed flat over her apron where the credstick sat against her ribs. Her arms hung rigid at her sides. Her gaze remained fixed on the sedan’s rear tires as they churned through the grey sludge of the alley, throwing muddy spray against the corrugated tin walls.
The suit sat in the leather seat opposite him, opening a briefcase lined with velvet compartments. He reached into a small sealed cylinder and took out a pink sugar drop, holding it out between gloved fingers.
“For the ride,” the suit said, his voice smooth and neutral. “Keep it on your tongue. It prevents nausea during transit.”
The candy tasted of synthetic strawberry and cold industrial solvent, slick on the palate like wet plastic. By the time the sedan cleared the corporate security gates at the Manila airfield, the sweet chemical coating had numbed the roof of the boy’s mouth, leaving behind only the sterile taste of air conditioning and clean leather.
Ji-yoo stood beneath the shivering metal eave in Redmond twenty years later, the same synthetic strawberry film coating the back of her teeth. The dull heat behind her cheekbones subsided into an ache that pulsed in time with her heartbeat. She spat the pink drop into the black sludge at the edge of the asphalt. It lay there, a small sphere of artificial color against the grime, before the sulfur rain began to wash its pink dye into the puddle.
She rolled her shoulders against the stiffness in her collarbone, pulled the heavy canvas collar tight against the damp wind coming off the Barrens, and stepped out into the dark.

title: Faceless Mirror
text:
The cauterizer in Whiskey’s Touristville basement clinic had a worn heating coil that emitted a high, thin whine every time her boot tapped the foot pedal. The sound competed with the heavy iron intake fan in the street-level window, which rattled against its security mesh whenever an automated freight hauler passed on the avenue above. Tanaka Ryo sat on the edge of the stainless steel examination table with his coarse linen shirt bunched in his lap, teeth set against the dry heat as Whiskey pressed the glowing copper tip against a flechette graze across his left shoulder blade. The wound had come from a territorial skirmish with Halloweeners near the Redmond border two nights earlier, a close call in the dark that had left his leather riding jacket shredded. He took the burn without local anesthetic, saving every certified nuyen to route through encrypted proxy accounts to Hana in Neo-Seoul.
“Hold your breath,” Whiskey muttered, her forehead beaded with sweat beneath the harsh glare of the overhead surgical lamp. She kept her eyes locked strictly on the three-inch line of torn muscle, working with the rapid, unblinking economy of a field medic under fire. She had not glanced at his face once since he climbed onto the table, her breath hissing through clenched teeth as the copper iron sizzled against living collagen, sealing the wound in dense, charred layers while Ryo sat unmoving beneath the light.
The singed heat against his shoulder skin brought back the antiseptic chill of the Mitsuhama post-op ward in Tokyo fifteen years before.
In the Tokyo facility, his entire head had been wrapped in damp smart-gauze that pulsed with automated saline flushes every twenty seconds. He was ten years old, lying on a narrow recovery cot in the dark, listening through the acoustic partition as the lead biometrics team reviewed his morning telemetry with the flat detachment of mechanics testing tolerances on an engine block. They spoke of cheekbone elevation, lash curvature, and the precise angle of the upper lip in fractions of a millimeter. A bound hermetic spirit drifted near the acoustic ceiling panels, stripped of name or ceremony—an enslaved industrial conduit casting an icy draft across the boy’s exposed shoulders as its mana circuits clamped the shaping formulas directly into his growing facial cartilage. Jin-Young stared into the woven black fibers of the bandages, his facial muscles twitching against fresh dissolvable sutures as the nerve pathways were chemically re-mapped to trigger a stranger’s smile.
For three weeks after the initial bone shaving, the smart-gauze remained sealed over his face, soaking in binding washes that carried the sharp scent of acetic acid and synthetic collagen. When the chief surgeon finally stepped into the ward to discharge him, her diagnostic specs projected thin emerald grids across his chest and throat. She signaled the orderlies with a flick of her stylus.
“Sutures dissolved,” she said, her voice flat against the hum of the air scrubbers. “The secondary cartilage binding took without tissue rejection. Remove the dressing.”
The assistants peeled the wraps with brisk, practiced motions, each layer coming away with the dry rasp of peeling parchment as the cool hospital air struck raw, newly formed skin with an icy burn. When the final layer dropped away, his skin pulled tight across cheekbones broad, heavy, and foreign.
“Check the baseline alignment,” the surgeon instructed. An assistant held up a rectangular mirror of polished, brushed steel before the cot.
Jin-Young looked into the metal.
The child who had played in the Manila monsoon was gone, replaced by a smooth, mathematically balanced face that belonged to no native bloodline. On the diagnostic monitor behind the cot, two digital profiles glowed side by side: the delicate, narrow jawline of Lee Ji-yoo and the broader, commanding symmetry of Tanaka Ryo. Both personas shared the same shaved foundation, a neutral biological canvas designed to pivot in either direction under the focus of cosmetic spells. Jin-Young raised a trembling hand, his fingertips touching skin smooth as polished stone, and tried to form the wide, gap-toothed grin his mother used to laugh at in the Tondo shanty. His facial muscles refused to cooperate. The nerves had been rerouted through corporate templates; when he forced the expression, his lips parted into a stiff, perfectly measured curve, the rehearsed idol smile now stamped into his living tissue.
“Baseline within designated parameters,” the surgeon noted, tapping her pad. “Archive the original facial scans. Prepare the asset for vocal modulation training.”
“Done,” Whiskey said in the Touristville clinic, her voice rough as she lifted the copper tip from his shoulder and dropped the cauterizer onto the metal tray with a sharp, echoing clatter. “Clean seal. Don’t stretch the deltoid for forty-eight hours, or you’ll rip the scab.”
She peeled the yellow latex gloves from her hands with two sharp snaps, throwing them into the biohazard bin beneath the counter, and unbuttoned her blood-speckled canvas smock. The moment the smock caught on the wall peg, the clinical rhythm of the room died, leaving only the hiss of the intake fan and the sudden, heavy silence between them.
She stepped over to the deep industrial sink, turned the cold brass tap, and thrust her bare forearms into the running water. When she lifted her hands, her fingers were visibly shaking—a raw autonomic tremor rattling her forearms. She clamped both palms hard against the stainless steel rim of the basin, locking her elbows and throwing her entire body weight onto the metal until her knuckles turned bloodless white against the steel. She stayed there, leaning over the drain with cold water splashing across her wrists, her breath coming in shallow and ragged as her nervous system struggled against the suffocating biological gravity filling the small room.
Behind her, Ryo pulled his coarse linen shirt over his head, the fabric catching slightly on the fresh scab as he walked to the grease-spotted mirror above the counter. The reflection staring back from the cracked glass was Tanaka Ryo: dark hair brushed back, jawline level, eyes clear and steady under the buzzing fluorescent tube. He leaned closer to the glass, looking where the outer rim of his pupils thinned in the downlight, revealing the faint, persistent ring of deep obsidian—the un-sculpted birth baseline waiting beneath the masks. He reached into his pocket and set two certified credsticks on the instrument tray beside the cooling iron, overpaying the street rate by half to cover the quiet deficit of her silence.
Whiskey did not look at the money. She kept her knuckles welded to the sink rim, staring down into the dark opening of the drain pipe as the cold water splashed over her wrists.
“You’re wearing the man today,” she said, her voice tight and strained against the heavy quiet in the basement. “It’s different. It’s too heavy in here.”
Ryo paused with his hand resting near the iron door latch. “Would it make it easier if I came in as Ji-yoo?”
“No,” she murmured, a low, raspy breath filtering through her teeth as she looked away from his reflection in the glass. “That might be worse. One of these days, you’re going to burn yourself down to the wire, and there won’t be enough skin left to sew back together.”
Ryo pushed open the heavy iron fire door and stepped out into the Touristville alley, letting the cold Seattle drizzle wash over smooth, unbroken skin without finding a single native crease to follow.

title: Dark Wings
text:
Under the hundred-thousand-watt daylight arrays of the Wuxing soundstage in Neo-Tokyo, the arena floor of Astral Athletics: Idol Showdown stretched across three acres of polished chrome obstacles, magnetized climbing lattices, and synchronized broadcast cameras. High in the acoustic rafters, fifty automated camera drones hovered like oversized beetles, tracking every metahuman leap and spell-assisted pivot for millions of viewers across the Pan-Asian Pacific feed. Tanaka Ryo stood at the western staging gantry in his unit’s charcoal and silver racing silks, his pulse held at a steady sixty beats per minute while the sub-floor transducers pumped synthetic adrenaline anthems through the reinforced decking.
The secondary transformer bank beneath the sub-floor let out a high-pitched acoustic scream, its cooling lines rupturing under the load of the high-voltage lighting grid. The main breaker tripped with an explosive crack, killing the daylight arrays in an instant and plunging the three-acre soundstage into sudden, suffocating darkness.
In the confusion of shouting floor directors, blaring static alarms, and rebooting security feeds, Ryo stepped off the staging gantry. Low-light filters in his retinas painted the dark corridors in sharp monochromatic grey. He moved through the backstage maze with unhurried, measured strides, his boots making no sound on the vibration-damped rubber flooring. Above the staging bays, the scent of vaporized transformer coolant and scorched fluoropolymer insulation drifted through the air vents, thick enough to mask his movement from the perimeter security dogs. He navigated two soundproofed access tunnels, reached the private VIP green room at the far end of the talent corridor, turned the brass latch, and pulled the heavy acoustic door shut behind him. The latch caught with a soft click, sealing the room against the external roar of the arena.
Luna sat in a low armchair in the far corner of the unlit room, her white stage silks catching the faint amber glow of an emergency exit sign above the private washroom. In the astral space near the acoustic ceiling panels, the bound watcher spirit tethered to Ryo’s aura drifted in a slow, circular patrol. The entity was an icy draft of corporate firmware, tracking his core temperature, his blood pressure, and the cadence of his respiration, programmed to ping Mitsuhama security in Kyoto at the first physiological deviation from his talent profile.
“You’re late,” Luna said. The voice was stripped of the airy, manufactured brightness broadcast across the weekly entertainment grids. A faint mechanical tick came from the cervical actuators in her neck as she turned her head toward him, her optical shutters clicking twice to adjust to the dim amber light.
“The secondary corridor had security patrols scanning talent passes,” Ryo said. The syllables slipped out in the soft, breathy cadence of Lee Ji-yoo before he caught himself, forcing his larynx down into Tanaka Ryo’s rigid baritone.
He sat on the arm of the leather sofa opposite her, resting his hands flat across his knees. In the absolute gloom, away from the staging lights and corporate lenses, the tension in his throat held between his assigned profiles. He deliberately released the cosmetic spell’s pressure on his jawline, letting the compressed cartilage settle into an aching, neutral middle. The bone-latch pressure behind his ears subsided into a dull, thrumming heat as the artificial symmetry relaxed into the raw baseline of his breath.
Luna raised a slender hand, her fingertips tracing the edge of her collarbone where Wuxing dermal plating met living skin. Thin chrome seams split the porcelain surface in the amber emergency glow, inlaid with microscopic silver serial numbers: WUX-EXP-884-LUNA.
“They adjusted the biometrics this morning,” she said, her voice flat against the hum of the wall scrubbers. “Lung capacity up twelve percent for the aerial choreography. My chest cavity feels hollow, like an empty tin can.”
“They plane the cartilage first,” he said, the softer elegance of Ji-yoo’s phrasing still bleeding into the lower register as his vocal cords rested. “Then the binding wash sets the tissue. It stays dry behind the ribs for the first year until the nerve endings stop firing.”
“Does it ever stop?” she asked, her eyes catching the faint red strobe from the ceiling smoke detector.
“No,” he said, the voice settling entirely into the un-sculpted baseline. “You learn to stop checking the mirror.”
Luna leaned forward, the white silk of her racing tunic rustling against the leather upholstery. Her shuttering optics fixed on his throat in the gloom, tracking the small, un-augmented pulse beating beneath smooth skin. She reached across the small space between their seats, her fingertips touching the back of his hand. Her skin was warm from the staging lights, but the fingers were rigid with micro-hydraulic joints that lacked the irregular, organic tremors of native flesh.
Through the physical contact, the hollow in her aura pressed against his astral senses. Most of her native essence had been hollowed out to seat reflex boosters, internal telemetry lines, and sensory processing chips, leaving behind an expanse of quiet emptiness framed by corporate chrome.
“You’re both,” she whispered, her voice barely carrying above the low hum of the corridor ventilation. “Aren’t you?”
The watcher spirit drifted closer in the astral plane, its icy aura brushing the hairs on the back of his neck as it sampled his galvanic skin response for signs of panic. Ryo kept his respiration perfectly level, timing his breaths to the sixty-beat pulse dictated by his biometric tracker while his thumb gently found the edge of her wrist.
Beneath the sub-floor, the heavy backup generator began to whine back to life, its low-frequency vibration rising through the floorboards. Emergency beacons along the baseboards flickered from amber to green.
“Hana,” she whispered into the dark between them. “My real name is Hana.” The syllables settled into the quiet room, un-stamped by corporate patent offices or marketing telemetry.
“Jin-Young,” he answered, his thumb pressing against the warm chrome seam where her hand met the wrist casing.
She pulled her hand back a fraction of a second before the main circuit caught. The soundstage flooded with blinding white light, washing the red shadows from the walls in a single pulse. When the Wuxing floor manager shoved the door open with a datapad in hand, Hana was already sitting upright with her posture straight and her chin lifted, eyes wide and smiling for the broadcast lens, while Tanaka Ryo stood by the door, his shoulders squared and his face locked back into immaculate corporate poise.

title: Sabotage
text:
The sub-floor dressing room beneath the Singapore mega-dome sat forty feet below the coastal water table, encased in six-foot slabs of vibration-dampened ferrocrete. Outside the climate envelope, the heavy equatorial heat of the Malacca Straits pressed against the reclaimed shoreline, but down in the prep trenches, the air was chilled to a dry, sterile eighteen degrees. Through the reinforced observation viewport overlooking the staging gantry, Tanaka Ryo watched two Mitsuhama corporate mages secure an inductive copper collar around Hana’s neck. The technicians worked in silence, their charcoal coats bearing the crimson triple-rhombus of Mitsuhama Media Logistics. Their sensor gloves glowed pale emerald as they calibrated the resonance couplings, tuning the frequencies until the secondary stage conduit hummed with a low, sub-audible vibration that rattled loose bolts in the deck plates.
Hana stood motionless on the prep riser under flickering mercury vapor tubes. Her porcelain dermal seams caught the harsh downlight, throwing sharp reflections across the bare concrete walls. Her chin stayed angled toward the overhead acoustic baffle, cervical actuators clicking at two-second intervals as internal micro-fans vented heat from her vocal processors. Across her collarbones, the corporate serial numbers were inlaid in microscopic silver foil: MCI-EXP-884-LUNA.
Beside Ryo’s vanity mirror, the stage logistics feed scrolled in amber characters across the glass: Unit 7 // Broadcast Apex // Full Resonance Extraction // Terminal Encore.
“Sixty seconds to lift locks,” the floor manager’s voice came through his earpiece, flat and clipped against the muffled seismic rumble overhead. “Ten-No-Koe choreography engages on the downbeat. Clear the gantry.”
Ryo stepped away from the glass. In the vanity mirror, Tanaka Ryo stared back: charcoal tunic tailored to the millimeter with silver silk piping, shoulders broadened by structural bio-sculpting, dark hair parted with razor-sharp corporate geometry. Beneath the immaculate exterior, his larynx carried the dull, grinding ache of the vocal shift, the cartilage held rigid against the instinct to soften into Lee Ji-yoo’s lighter cadence. He checked the magnetic seals on his stage cuffs. High above his left shoulder in the astral space, the bound watcher spirit hovered—a cold draft that tracked his core temperature, his blood pressure, and the cadence of his pulse, reporting every physiological deviation straight to the security node in Kyoto.
“Ten seconds,” the floor manager said.
Ryo walked out onto the central staging platform. The copper conductor plate under his boots was chilled from the subterranean cooling coils, etched with concentric geometric spirals that channeled directly into the primary geomantic lines running beneath the arena foundation. Ji-Hoon stood at the northern riser, his chrome forearm casings gleaming under the staging floods. Tae-Hyun adjusted his lacquered wolf mask at the eastern mark, while Min-Ki checked his footing on the western boundary plate. None of them spoke. Speech outside the designated broadcast telemetry carried automatic behavioral penalty deductions against their quarterly talent trusts.
The lift engaged with a heavy hydraulic hiss. The sub-floor acoustic drivers pumped seventy tons of sound pressure through the alloy platform, vibrating straight through his shins into his jaw. The lift breached the stage deck, rising through the floor into the blinding glare of the daylight arrays. Eighty-five thousand voices hit him like a physical wall. The crowd packed the tiered terraces beneath the smart-glass dome, a vast sea of synchronized glow-sticks and flashing AR banners undulating under the humid equatorial haze. Mitsuhama Media corporate holograms fifty feet high rotated in the stadium airspace, projecting the idol unit’s faces into the clouds.
The downbeat dropped. The choreography seized the unit with automated precision. Ji-Hoon hit the northern apex, limbs snapping into position as his internal cybernetics hummed in sync with the heavy synth-percussion. Tae-Hyun drove the eastern harmony, his wolf mask throwing sharp blue shadows across the first twenty rows, while Min-Ki anchored the western perimeter. Ryo crossed the center mark on count four, boots planting on the central conductor plate as the opening vocal line began.
The circuit closed. Eighty-five thousand minds surged into the channel. The sensation struck like a river of liquid fire. The geomantic siphon opened wide across the arena floor, harvesting the raw, uncritical adoration of eighty-five thousand spectators and funneling that emotional tidal wave straight through the stage risers. As the unit’s lead channel, Ryo became the biological lightning rod. The manufactured euphoria tore through his meridians with terrifying heat, expanding his aura until the spirit ribbons of his Musok training frayed under the sheer volume of collective desire. His voice rose into the arena’s quad-directional acoustic array, pure and effortless, riding the crest of the chorus while the telemetry monitors in his peripheral vision spiked deep into the red.
Through the white glare of the pyro flares, the secondary lift crested the stage floor. Hana rose on the sacrificial riser, framed in shimmering white brocade. The instant the staging conduit touched her copper collar, her cervical actuators locked with a sharp metallic snap. Her jaw was pulled upward, throat exposed to the daylight arrays as the Mitsuhama extraction protocol began tearing into her spiritual baseline. The crowd roared in response, mistaking her rigid, trembling posture and the radiant aura flare around her shoulders for an advanced holographic effect. The collective adoration of eighty-five thousand fans, channeled through Ryo’s voice, was being compressed and focused into her neck collar, stripping her essence to charge the corporate geomantic batteries buried in the arena foundation.
Ryo hit his turnaround at bar sixteen, spinning toward the center riser. Through the swirling stage smoke and strobes, he fixed on the porcelain seam along her cheek. Her breathing came in short, shallow gasps. Her eyes were wide, the optical shutters cycling erratically as the circuit burned through her neural firmware.
Then her gaze shifted, cutting through the sweep of automated broadcast drones, and locked directly onto his face.
The rehearsed stage-smile dropped from her lips. In the two seconds before the chorus peaked, her mouth formed a quiet, crooked curve—an un-scripted expression of recognition that answered his silence and released him from his marks.
Holding his position for eight more bars would allow the extraction to complete cleanly, leaving Hana an empty shell in the medical ward while Tanaka Ryo returned to his penthouse with his corporate contract intact. The logistics division would file the incident as an acute resonance burnout during a historic performance, paying out a modest survivor stipend to her registered relatives in Neo-Seoul.
At the crescendo, as eighty-five thousand voices crested in a synchronized roar, Ryo broke alignment. He dropped his chin, clamped his teeth until his jaw joints ground together, and wrenched the flow inward. He planted his heels hard against the copper plate, twisting his ankles to short-circuit the grounding trace, and routed eighty-five thousand channels of raw, un-buffered emotional energy straight into his own bone and adept channels, severing the feed to the stage capacitors.
The backlash struck like an iron slab through his skull. His spirit conduits surged against the flood, spirit ribbons violently untangling as the sheer volume of un-filtered mana overloaded his nervous system. The inductive copper plate beneath his boots superheated, the alloy warping with a screech of shearing rivets. The synthetic leather of his boots melted into smoldering resin against his soles. White sparks showered the front rows. Along the perimeter of the dome, the geomantic storage capacitors detonated in a sequence of deafening concussions, tearing structural pylons from their concrete footings and blowing fifty-foot sheets of flame into the access corridors.
The arena transformers screamed and blew. The Singapore mega-dome plunged into total, suffocating darkness. The music died mid-note, replaced by the sound of tearing speakers and eighty-five thousand voices collapsing from synthetic euphoria into blind, stampeding panic under the shattered ceiling.
Ryo hit the smoking stage deck. The electrical surge tore through his chest, locking his lungs in a violent spasm while the acrid stench of scorched insulation and vaporized circuit boards filled the air. Red emergency beacons flickered to life along the catwalks, painting the rising smoke in bloody streaks. Through the haze, corp-sec alarms began their rhythmic wail. Tactical mages in the wings shouted over dead radio channels, scrambling to contain the crowd as the smart-glass dome above began to crack under the acoustic shockwave.
He rolled off the shattered riser, landing hard in the debris-filled service trench beneath the stage platform. Blistered fingers dragged across jagged concrete until they hooked the iron ring of a drainage hatch. He hauled the iron cover back with a guttural heave and dropped into the dark.
He plunged into waist-deep brackish seawater and industrial runoff in the storm culvert beneath the arena foundation. The cold hit his scorched skin like a sheet of needles. In the pitch blackness of the sewer, Ryo ripped the smoking Mitsuhama tunic from his shoulders, tearing the embroidered silver piping and letting the oil-slicked water wash away the stage foundation and grey streaks of sweat from his neck. Above him, the rumble of the panicked stadium faded into the distant drone of harbor sirens.
The bound watcher spirit was gone, incinerated in the geomantic backlash. His commlink lay dead in the sludge. Wading against the tide of seawater, hands stinging from fresh electrical burns across his palms, Ryo pushed through the subterranean channels toward the container docks at Jurong—nameless, stripped of his corporate skin, and stepping into the shadows on his own terms.

title: First Negotiation
text:
Tanaka Ryo kept the unbadged Suzuki idling between his knees in the Redmond alley, the engine’s rhythmic vibration rattling loose fairing bolts against the cold steel frame. Across the polarized visor of his Shoei helmet, pirated AR spam flickered through the sulfur drizzle, with glitching advertisements for Stuffer Shack ramen and second-hand cyberware fighting for bandwidth in the local mesh. The exhaust pipe gave off a faint metallic ping as it cooled against the wet air. He cut the ignition with a turn of the key but left the helmet locked down tight over his chin; in the Barrens, bare features were an invitation to street violence, while features sculpted with corporate symmetry were a magnetic disturbance that drew eyes from across a crowded room.
Inside the Red Line, sub-floor bass vibrated through the grease-stained floorboards from a jukebox looping thirty-year-old Neo-Tokyo synth-pop. Still wearing the dark, faceless dome of his riding helmet, he paused near a dead arcade terminal in the corner, shoulders slouched to mimic a delivery courier waiting on a delayed package. In the back booth beneath a flickering Shiawase promotional banner sat the Johnson, wearing a surplus wool overcoat with the frayed stitch scars of a NeoNet security patch cut from the lapel. The man nursed a glass of amber synthetic rye, his eyes darting between the front door and the bar taps with the ingrained nervousness of an ex-corporate middle manager stranded outside the grid.
Through the smoked shield of his visor, Ryo watched him in the scratched reflection of the arcade glass. When a heavy-set ork mercenary in armored ballistic plates pushed past the aisle, the Johnson’s aura flared with jagged, defensive orange, his right hand twitching toward an illegal pocket holster beneath his coat. But when the bar’s floor manager stepped over to clear an empty beer bottle, the man’s posture shifted instinctively—his spine straightened, chin dipping into the reflexive, ingrained deference of a salaryman accustomed to taking directives from executive suites. A heavy masculine runner would trigger his panic and draw a defensive standoff, whereas a corporate woman with clean, icy composure would slide beneath his guard and command the table.
Ryo slipped past the bar toward the narrow corridor leading to the rear storage rooms. The restroom was a damp concrete cell lit by a single buzzing fluorescent tube that threw grey shadows across stained tile, where cold water dripped steadily from an overhead copper pipe into a cracked ceramic urinal. He locked the iron latch, unclipped the Shoei helmet, and set it on the water tank before stripping off his heavy riding leathers. He initiated the shift as his Transys Avalon commlink re-keyed the local PAN registers to broadcast the clean, forged SIN of Lee Ji-yoo. The physical toll struck his marrow with dry, burning friction as the cosmetic spell engaged: Ryo gripped the cold porcelain edges of the sink, knuckles whitening as structural magic compressed his ribcage with a grinding ache, vertebra settling against vertebra while cartilage in his larynx aligned with a heavy click that thinned his breath to a lighter register.
She opened her eyes in the stained mirror, waiting three slow breaths for the momentary vertigo to clear while the bone-latch behind her ears cooled. She smoothed the dark silk shell over her narrowed shoulders, left the heavy riding jacket folded behind the exposed water pipes, and stepped into flat leather shoes. Unlocking the iron door, she walked back into the smoky gloom of the bar with the quiet, acoustic poise of an executive assistant entering a boardroom, slipping into the booth opposite the Johnson with silent, fluid grace. The man looked up, his hand freezing on the rim of his glass as the red neon from the bar sign caught her face—clean, balanced, without a single blemish, scar, or line of street fatigue. His throat moved as he swallowed, fingers slipping off the synthetic rye as his nervous system struggled to recalibrate under the sudden, focused weight of her presence.
“You’re late,” he said, but the words carried no weight against the stillness across the table.
“Knight Errant sweeps were active along the perimeter highway,” Ji-yoo said, her voice clear, level, and entirely devoid of street slang. “The transit took longer to avoid automated checkpoints.”
The Johnson cleared his throat, wiped a sheen of cold sweat from his palm against his wool trousers, and slid a battered Sony datapad across the cedar laminate. “Renraku storage node in Bellevue. Ten thousand nuyen. Five thousand up front for operational expenses, five on delivery.”
Ji-yoo glanced at the encrypted node coordinates on the screen, then rested her hands flat and open on the table. “Eight thousand,” she said.
The Johnson blinked, his brow furrowing as he leaned back. “What?”
“Eight thousand,” she repeated, her tone calm and conversational. “And no advance.”
The Johnson pulled back into the corner of the booth, his eyes narrowing with sharp corporate suspicion. Street runners fought over every scrip, demanding up-front deposits for ammo, forged credentials, and decker fees. A runner who negotiated the price downward was an operative with an unstated agenda.
“Runners don’t negotiate down,” the Johnson said, his grip tightening on the table edge. “Who are you working for?”
“Clean retrieval,” Ji-yoo said, holding his gaze with unblinking composure. “Renraku will not log the intrusion as an external breach. When the datapad is delivered, you owe me a marker. One favor, on demand, within your departmental authority.”
The Johnson sat motionless. The immediate relief of saving corporate operating budget died, replaced by the heavy understanding of personal debt. Nuyen was spent and forgotten; a personal marker was much longer lasting. He looked at the quiet poise across the table, the complete absence of street desperation, and gave a single, tight nod.
“One marker,” he said, sliding the pad fully across the wood. “We have an agreement.”
Ji-yoo picked up the datapad, slipped it into her coat pocket, and stood. She walked out into the Redmond drizzle, leaving the Johnson alone with his synthetic rye beneath the glitching neon.

title: Seattle Web
text:
From the flat gravel roof of the four-story Redmond tenement, the Wuxing needle cut a slender emerald mark against the low sulfur cloud cover over downtown Seattle. Cold rain drummed steadily against the rusted corrugated housing of an industrial roof exhaust, pooling in grease-stained puddles around his boots. He sat on the iron casing with his Transys Avalon commlink resting between his knees, its diagnostic display casting pale blue light across his wet leather riding trousers. Thirty feet below in the alleyway, the muffled hum of a pirated power transformer vibrated through the brickwork, competing with the distant, mournful wail of a Knight Errant patrol siren out on the perimeter highway.
To lock the encrypted transmission against local grid sweeps and avoid astral resonance reflections, he released the spells he was holding. The shaping magic drained from his facial tissue in a cold, prickling wave. Ribs widened with a deep, grinding ache as his chest expanded to its native volume, the compressed bone settling into its true frame with an audible creak. Cartilage along his jawline broadened with a heavy, wet click, the artificial symmetry of Tanaka Ryo dissolving as solid obsidian pigment pooled back into the outer rims of his irises. For the first time in three weeks, the metabolic burn behind his temples ceased, allowing him to pull air through the raw, un-sculpted lungs of Kim Jin-Young while sulfur-tinged damp hit his bronchial lining without corporate filtration. He wiped water from the commlink’s optical pickup with the dry inner lining of his sleeve and initiated the encrypted hand-shake protocol.
The transmission signal jumped through three separate dead-letter relays across Denver, Vladivostok, and Hong Kong before locking onto a private optical node in the Neo-Seoul network. The Avalon’s holo-emitter whirred with a high-pitched acoustic whine, projecting a high-resolution terminal feed through the falling rain while light refracted through the wet air, throwing shimmering blue and gold halos across the gravel rooftop. The display stabilized into crisp, three-dimensional light. Hana sat in an opulent, high-floor executive suite within the Wuxing Seoul Arcology, framed by floor-to-ceiling smart-glass looking out over the glowing neon sea of the Gangnam district. Outside her window, fifty-story holographic billboards cast shifting crimson and violet hues across the polished marble floor. She wore a tailored white silk blazer over an emerald blouse, her dark hair swept up and secured with antique jade pins, while dermal plating along her collarbones gleamed beneath warm architectural lighting where silver asset serial numbers were polished like fine jewelry: WUX-EXP-884-LUNA. Her cervical actuators were completely silent, upgraded to executive-grade hydraulic silent-runners that produced no mechanical tick when she tilted her head.
“Jin-Young,” she said, her voice rich, resonant, and entirely stripped of the breathy fragility he remembered from the soundstages. Her optical shutters cycled once, tracking the low-light feed from the Redmond roof.
“The routing is clean,” he said, speaking in his unmasked baseline voice. “The courier in Tacoma cleared the credstick drop yesterday. Twelve thousand nuyen in certified scrip. It should cover the medical retainer for your cervical servos through the winter.”
Hana looked directly into the camera array, her expression composed with the serene, untouchable authority of a corporate vice-president reviewing quarterly performance charts. “You shouldn’t have called,” she said quietly. “And you shouldn’t have sent the money.”
His fingers tightened on the alloy edge of the commlink casing, rain dripping from his chin onto the polarized glass. He leaned toward the emitter lens, holding his breath as the cold water soaked through his collar. “The courier had clean credentials from the docks,” he said, keeping his baseline tone level. “What happened?”
“Wuxing didn’t intercept the drop, Jin,” she said, her voice smooth and devoid of panic. “They cleared the payment through their primary banking node. Your entire courier chain in Seattle operates on their talent retention budget.” The rain seemed to grow heavier around him, washing over the gravel in cold, grey sheets that flattened his hair against his forehead. “Mitsuhama and Wuxing signed a joint security accord three months ago,” she continued, her gaze steady across the trans-Pacific link. “They aren’t hunting you through the Barrens with tactical kill-teams. They promoted me to senior creative director for Pan-Asian Media. My face is projected across fifty-story holograms in every sector from Neo-Tokyo to Singapore. They gave me this suite, these upgrades, and this title because their actuarial models calculated that your emerging empathy would keep you looking back.”
A cold, hollow stillness opened in the center of his chest, aching far deeper than the physical shifting of bone. “Every payment you sent through Tacoma, every encrypted relay you bought from Seattle deckers, and every shadow contract you completed was logged on a Wuxing server,” she said, her fingers tapping the arm of her white leather chair where chrome nail beds flashed in the golden lamplight. “They used your concern as the exact breadcrumb trail to map your entire network in the sprawl. They know your safehouses, your contacts, and your street docs. The contracts to reclaim both of us under joint corporate ownership are already drafted and sitting on the board table.”
Jin-Young sat motionless in the dark, the rain soaking through his collar, freezing against the bare skin of his neck. Every gesture of emerging care had been logged, indexed, and converted into corporate telemetry. The megacorps commodified his empathy, turning his refusal to be a corporate product into the very snare designed to drag him back into the trainee dormitories.
“They’re waiting for you to exhaust yourself,” Hana said, her voice softening by a fraction of a degree, though her eyes remained locked on the camera. “When you realize you can’t run far enough, they expect you to walk into the Seattle consulate and sign the joint agreement.” When he opened his mouth, the syllable of her true name died in his dry throat. “My name is Director Yueying now,” she said, the polite, unbreakable corporate smile returning to her porcelain lips, cold as glazed ceramic. “Do not transmit to this node again.” The holo-emitter cut out with a sharp pop, plunging the roof back into the dark.
Jin-Young sat in the rain as the sulfur wind came off the Barrens, listening to the water drum against the rusted sheet metal eaves while in the distance across the bay, the emerald needle of the Wuxing tower pulsed through the low clouds, cold, immense, and untouchable above the sprawl. He stood up, wet gravel grinding beneath the soles of his boots. He dropped the Transys Avalon commlink onto the concrete, raised his heel, locked his knee, and drove the heavy riding sole down into the alloy casing until the glass shattered, the motherboard buckled, and the optical processors died in a brief shower of orange sparks. He kicked the crushed scrap into the rain gutter, pulled his collar high against the damp wind, and walked toward the fire escape. He took the metal stairs down into the dark, stepping off the surface grid and heading deep into the Seattle underground.

title: Bliss
text:
Beneath the West Seattle elevated freight overpass, automated Ares Macrotechnology cargo haulers rumbled across steel expansion joints every sixty seconds, sending a deep shudder through the rusted framework of the roadside noodle cart. Cold rain dripped from the torn vinyl awning into the curb drain, hissing against the cast-iron burner where forty gallons of rich pork-bone broth simmered in a heavy aluminum cauldron. In the wet air, holographic AR banners from Shiawase Logistics and Yakashima Food Services flickered and glitched across the concrete pillars, casting jagged amber reflections in oil-slicked puddles. Velvet sat on the corner wooden stool, wrapped in a dark oilskin slicker, wearing the street persona of Mei Jing. Faded blue syndicate ink traced the tendons of her right wrist and rose along the left side of her jaw beneath the upturned canvas collar, anchoring her physical presence in the dockside working class.
On the cedar counter next to her steaming bowl sat the credstick basket from the Octagon Triad courier, holding in the corner of its weave a single unopened Bliss capsule wrapped in silver yin-yang foil—fifteen nuyen of synthetic chemical numbness meant as a gratuity for the courier’s run. She picked up the small cylinder, turning the plastic between her bare fingers before setting it back beside the broth while across the counter. The elderly cook lowered fresh wheat noodles into boiling water with a wire basket, the rising steam creating a warm, clouded pocket of air that held the sulfur rain at bay.
Water splashed in the gutter as heavy boots dragged along the broken asphalt, and a man stumbled into the shelter of the awning wearing a waterlogged Ares work jacket where the Russian Vory insignia on the left shoulder had been violently hacked off with a combat blade, leaving frayed grey threads hanging over torn ballistic weave.
He slumped onto the stool two seats away, raw, bruised hands trembling against the wooden counter as he fought to steady his respiration. “Broth,” the man rasped, his vocal cords raw from the aftereffects of inhaled aerosol sedatives. “Hot.” The cook slid a heavy ceramic bowl across the cedar wood without asking for creds up front, but when the man reached for bamboo chopsticks from the stoneware jar, his twitching fingers lost their grip, sending the sticks clattering across the wet laminate. He stared down at his swollen knuckles, his forearms still suffering involuntary tremors from the Narcoject autoinjector Velvet had driven into his cervical cluster thirty-six hours earlier. When he turned his head slowly, bloodshot eyes fixed on the woman sitting two stools away, his breath caught in his throat as he recognized the faded triad ink along her jawline and the unnerving, motionless calm in her dark eyes. His right hand jerked instinctively toward an empty armpit holster, his eyes wide with terror.
The man was Pavel, the young Vory combat mage who had broken under fire as the perimeter wards collapsed around the illicit narcotics refinery. “You,” Pavel whispered, his voice trembling as he pressed his spine hard against the cart’s iron support pole.
Velvet kept her hands open beside her ceramic bowl, meeting his panic with quiet, grounded stillness. “Drink the broth,” she said, her voice low, steady, and carrying the soothing, resonant cadence of Lee Ji-yoo. “The chili oil clears the chemical residue from the bronchial lining.”
Pavel swallowed hard, his chest heaving under the damp canvas jacket as he looked between her open hands and the steaming soup. “I know the containment formulas,” he blurted out, the words spilling past his lips in a rush of shame and exhausted panic. “I bound a hearth-spirit when I was fourteen in Vladivostok. I had the chalk circle drawn on the concrete. But the mana tore away the second I spoke the binding mantra. The spirit wouldn’t take form. Before your strike team breached the iron doors, my magic was already dead in my hands. If the Vory elders think I choked on a basic third-circle summon, they’ll weigh my boots with scrap iron and dump me in the Duwamish river before sunrise.”
Velvet looked at the young mage, his skin grey and hollow under the single yellow work bulb hanging from the cart awning. She picked up her bowl, letting the ceramic heat soak into her palms. “The geothermal plant was built directly over the Puyallup ash beds,” Velvet said quietly, her tone matter-of-fact and calm. “Surrounded by subterranean coal fires, heavy industrial slag, and un-filtered chemical runoff from the old Renraku smelters, the ground water beneath the floor was saturated with industrial mercury. The local background count was screaming toxic pollution. Your chalk circle was structurally intact and your vocal gesture was clean, but the mana broke because the earth beneath your boots was poisoned. No hermetic mage in Seattle summons a clean spirit out of industrial sewage. You took a sedative dart during the initial breach and lost consciousness while holding the northern access corridor. Tell that story, and keep your head down.”
Pavel sat completely motionless on the stool as the white-knuckled grip on his knees relaxed, letting out a long, ragged breath that mixed with the rising steam from the aluminum cauldron. He looked down at his hands, finding them steady for the first time in two days, then picked up a fresh pair of chopsticks from the jar, dipped them into the dark broth, and pulled noodles to his mouth. They sat together beneath the rattling awning as the rain poured over the West Seattle overpass, eating hot noodles in the quiet shelter away from the sprawl, leaving the silver Bliss capsule untouched in the credstick basket.

title: Tea in Tacoma
text:
Salt fog off Commencement Bay rolled up the dark slope of the Tacoma waterfront, wrapping around the low wooden eaves of Xingfu Chaguan and muffling the rhythmic clang of container cranes out in the deep-water harbor. Inside the private rear tea room, the mechanical roar of the industrial sprawl fell away, replaced by the gentle hiss of water reaching a simmer in a cast-iron kettle over a bed of glowing hardwood charcoal. Old-growth cedar panels lined the walls, insulated with acoustic damping and copper mesh that blocked external Matrix feeds, wireless transceivers, and optical surveillance drones. The air carried the dry, earthy fragrance of roasted oolong and warm cedar resin.
Tanaka Ryo sat on a low tatami cushion across from Ni Ni Xiaolu, his posture held in his masculine baseline profile, shoulders square under an unbadged charcoal silk overcoat. Across the low cedar table, Ni Ni Xiaolu sat with immaculate poise in a tailored black blazer over ivory silk, her dark hair swept up and fastened with antique bone pins. She watched him over the rim of a small celadon cup, the stillness in her frame carrying the hard-won vigilance of an Octagon Triad Red Pole who had survived three separate syndicate purges along the Seattle waterfront.
Between them on the cedar wood, resting precisely six inches from her right hand, lay her customized Ares Predator heavy pistol, its mother-of-pearl grip catching the amber glow of the charcoal burner. Outside the rice-paper sliding door, the heavy silhouette of Teddy Chin stood post in the corridor, his cybernetic arms crossed over his chest.
Ni Ni set the clay teapot down with a soft, deliberate click against the cedar tray. “The Cutters have pulled their enforcers back from the West Seattle bridge,” she said, her voice smooth, level, and quiet in the enclosed space. “Bookie’s Ancients agreed to keep their bike patrols east of the river. And Baxter’s bootleg Bliss refinery in Puyallup is cold slag.”
She paused, her dark eyes fixing on the calm symmetry of his face with sharp, analytical appraisal.“My courier brought back the credstick basket from the noodle cart,” she continued, her tone conversational yet probing. “You left the Bliss capsule on the street.”
“Counterfeits poison the market, Ms. Xiaolu,” Ryo said, his voice resonant and steady. “Yours and mine. An asset who relies on synthetic numbness makes mistakes on the operational perimeter.”
Ni Ni studied him across the rising steam, tracking the steady line of his jaw, the complete absence of nervous micro-tremors, and the quiet focus in his dark eyes. “Who engineered you, Mr. Tanaka?” she asked softly. “Was it Mitsuhama? Or did Wuxing send a bio-sculpted asset to listen through my cedar walls?”
Her right hand slid across the polished cedar table, her manicured fingers coming to rest lightly over the pearl grip of the heavy Predator.
Ryo did not reach for an internal holster, nor did the muscles in his neck tighten into a defensive posture. He deliberately allowed his active presence to settle into neutral stillness, releasing the subtle spell-tension behind his jaw. He reached out with bare, steady hands, lifted his celadon cup, and took a slow sip of the dark, steaming tea.
“No corporation sent me to you, Ms. Xiaolu,” Ryo said, setting the cup back onto the cedar tray without making a sound. He met her gaze across the table, his hands resting open and flat on the wood. “I operate in the shadows to pay for my refusal to take directives from corporate boardrooms.”
Silence settled across the cedar-lined room, filled only by the quiet bubbling of the iron kettle and the distant, mournful groan of a foghorn out in the bay. Ni Ni’s fingers remained on the pearl weapon grip for three slow, measured breaths. Then her hand withdrew, settling flat in her lap beneath the edge of the table.
Her shoulders sank slightly, the rigid tension along her collarbone easing as she lifted her teapot with both hands, pouring a fresh stream of amber liquid into his cup.
“The leaves are harvested from old bushes near Ningbo,” she murmured, watching the steam rise against the wood ceiling. “Smuggled across the Pacific in dry cargo containers without corporate tariffs.”
“It tastes of clean iron and rain,” Ryo said, nodding in quiet appreciation.
They sat together in the warm, cedar-lined room as the Puget Sound drizzle drummed softly against the roof tiles, drinking un-monetized tea in the quiet space away from the sprawl. When Ryo stood to depart, he left two certified credsticks on the edge of the table for the tea master, bowed with respectful corporate economy, and stepped out into the cold Tacoma salt fog.

title: Heat
text:
The oily smoke of the incinerator barrel thinned into the North Sea drizzle, leaving only a crust of melted ballistic weave and charred resin at the bottom of the rusted drum. Across the canal, the yellow floodlights of the Europort terminal sliced through the fog, silhouetting the massive gantry cranes of Ruhrmetall Logistics as they stacked automated freight containers with rhythmic, hydraulic thuds. Velvet watched the last scrap of blood-spattered synthetic cotton burn to gray ash before stepping back into the shelter of the quay wall.
With a subvocal tap against the throat mic, Velvet cued Ai-chan. The commlink app, an enterprise Personal Assistant package hosted on the Erika Elite, instantly engaged its client-side graphics pipeline. It was no sentient digital mind, merely a ruthlessly efficient model parsing network telemetry, monitoring local sensor feeds, and orchestrating tools across Velvet’s personal area network. Ai-chan queried the ambient lighting parameters, calculated the refractive index of the falling rain, and projected a tailored navy cashmere trench over Velvet’s shoulders. To any dockworker or harbor drone scanning the wharf, the illusion was immaculate, complete with crisp lapels, realistic wool physics, and matte silver buttons catching the sodium glare. Beneath the holographic light, however, the damp Dutch gale bit straight into the bare SecureTech skinshield, slick with sulfur residue.
Even with a fire ancestor coaxed into the hearth of the ribs, the North Sea chill worked into the marrow. The ancestral spirit rested warm against the sternum, radiating dry, talismanic heat that kept the blood moving, but it could not stop sixty kilometers of maritime damp from clinging to exposed skin.
Velvet pushed through the frosted glass door of De Vries & Zoon, an outfitter tucked between two freight forwarders along the canal quay. Radiator heat carried the alkaline bite of dry tailoring chalk and hot lanolin from the bolts overhead, heavy enough to push back the bitter chicory simmering in an enamel pot behind the counter. Rolls of double-faced Antwerp wool and oiled sea-canvas were stacked to the acoustic tile ceiling, deadening the low-frequency thrum of container tugs out in the basin.
Behind the basting table, an elderly tailor in a corduroy vest looked up, a yellowed wooden measuring tape resting across his stooped shoulders. The man wiped his steel shears with an oily rag, his pale eyes cataloging Velvet’s posture with the indifferent precision of an old port tradesman.
“Closed in ten,” the tailor said in Flemish-accented English, laying the shears on a cutting block. “Unless you take off the rack.”
“Off the rack is fine,” Velvet said. The syllables came out in Lawrence Duval’s precise, continental French cadence, though the sudden shift forced a dull ache through the base of the skull as the larynx cartilage settled into the new vocal register. “Charcoal overcoat. Heavy knit underneath. Something that moves quietly through customs offices.”
The tailor stepped from behind the laminate counter and reached out to gauge the shoulder seam of Duval’s navy trench. His dry, calloused fingers passed straight through the holographic projection, striking the cold, synthetic polymer of the skinshield beneath.
The old man pulled his hand back smoothly, squinting through the blue wireframe of the AR garment at the bare torso and the faint red telemetry markers Ai-chan was flashing along the dermal seams.
“The light show is very modern, meneer,” the tailor murmured, his tone as dry as pumice. “Very sharp for a video meet in Brussels, but light does not stop fifty kilometers of Maas wind.”
“No,” Duval said softly. A silent subvocal impulse to Ai-chan dissolved the navy blazer into the yellow bulb-light of the shop, leaving only the neutral, charcoal-grey line of the skinshield against the damp pine floorboards. “It does not.”
The tailor measured the scorch marks along the dermal sleeve with a single indifferent flick of his thumb before turning to the wall rack. In a port city where cargo went missing between Ghent and Europort every night, an unclad customer with certified creds was merely another Tuesday transaction. He pulled a heavy bolt of double-faced Belgian wool from the rack, unrolling three yards across the basting board with a satisfying, muffled thud.
“Stand on the round,” the old man grunted, nodding toward a low oak pedestal before a three-panel dressing mirror.
Velvet stepped onto the wood. As the cold brass tips of the measuring tape brushed collarbone and spine, Velvet shifted his features subtly. Beneath the living skin, the biological levers responded to conscious will: the jawline squared a fraction of a millimeter to support Duval’s crisp Gallic vowels, the clavicle broadened to hold the heavier drape of European tailoring, and the ribcage compressed slightly to steady the lungs. The internal bone-latch clicked deep behind the ear, a brief spike of metabolic heat swallowed without a flinch.
In the three-panel mirror, the lingering ghost of the previous forty-eight hours seemed to flicker against the glass. In Ghent, two automated freight trucks loaded with mass-produced, smiling green dragon plushies had been bought with a Saeder-Krupp Johnson’s caved-in skull and the deafening clatter of heavy machine gun fire. Yet forty minutes before the shooting tore the loading dock apart, beside a muddy canal pitch, Velvet had watched hardened syndics drop their weapons to shout for their children in the sudden downpour. The memory settled deep behind Duval’s newly sculpted eyes, anchoring the quiet, stubborn endurance of ordinary people surviving in the shadow of corporate titans.
The tailor tossed a charcoal overcoat over Duval’s shoulders. The weight hit with immediate, anchoring force, ten pounds of dense, boiled wool pressing the fire ancestor’s warmth back into the chest. The scratch of the raw fiber against the neck was abrasive, grounding, and completely real.
The old man pinned the left cuff with three swift jabs of his needle. “Good wool has memory,” he muttered, smoothing the back seam with the flat of his palm. “You treat it right, it holds the shape of the man wearing it long after the weather breaks.”
“Let us hope so,” Duval said, sliding his arms through the heavy silk lining and stepping down from the pedestal. “Monsieur, if I may ask. Word around the quay is that the dock families were stirred up after what happened in Ghent. I had hoped to make their acquaintance before my transport departs.”
The tailor paused, smoothing the chalk line along the lapel before looking up. “A messy business near the rail yards. S-K security drones have been buzzing the canal since dawn. Best not to ask questions near the cranes. Best not to be seen.”
“I agree completely,” Duval replied with a faint, polite inclination of the head. “And yet, a man in my line of trade cannot leave the Maas without speaking to the people who control the water.”
The old man tapped the end of his wooden tape against his palm, weighing the cut of the wool against the French accent. “Walk four blocks past the lock gate. There is a bathhouse behind the eel smoker with a red tile roof and no Matrix sign. The dock stewards go there to sweat out the cold and wash the diesel from their hair. Tell the girl at the counter that Pieter sent you for the birch steam. If anyone is willing to talk business while S-K sweeps the harbor, you will find them there.”
Velvet pulled three certified credsticks from the commlink pouch, laid them on the basting table with extra for discretion, and buttoned the heavy wool coat to the throat. Stepping out into the sulfuric Europort fog, the North Sea wind slammed against the heavy Belgian wool and broke harmlessly against it, leaving the vessel inside dry, warm, and entirely opaque.

title: Burns
text:
The copper wash-vats in the basement beneath the Sham Shui Po apothecary simmered over low gas rings, filling the narrow stone cellar with the pungent, stinging steam of boiled white vinegar and crushed camphor leaves. Above the low rafters, the rhythmic clatter of the morning industrial laundry sent fine plaster dust drifting through the damp air, settling across rolls of unbleached cotton gauze and rusted zinc tubs. Velvet sat on an overturned tea crate in the corner, elbows resting on his knees, breathing in the sour heat to scour the taste of scorched insulation from the back of his throat.
Stripping away two distinct lives in less than six hours had extracted an unforgiving biological tax.
The elder dignity of Zhang Wei had died first, shattered in the cordite haze and splintered shelving of the Jade Crane storage facility when the Red Dragon enforcers drew down. Then, on the rain-slicked concrete of Kwai Chung lot CT4, Leung Hoi-ching’s working-class harbor existence had been incinerated under the blinding, concussive fury of a summoned gale. When the air spirit’s lightning arced across the container stacks, strobing the berths in violet-white, fleeing syndicate soldiers had caught Hoi-ching’s face under the security floods just as corporate security patrol sirens began their wail.
Velvet reached up with bare, trembling fingers, unfastening the stained high-visibility vest and grease-marked linen shirt of the harbor clerk. He dropped them into the iron drain at his feet and released the active spell-work.
The cosmetic matrix dissolved from his facial tissue with a dry, searing heat. Deep within the zygomatics, the compressed bone-latches released, clicking heavily through the skull as his facial geometry widened. The broadened mandibular frame and shortened clavicles of Hoi-ching eased back into their natural alignment, spinal vertebrae settling with a dull, grinding throb that radiated down into his lower back. He closed his eyes against the sharp migraine behind his temples, waiting as the dark obsidian pigment flooded back into the outer rings of his irises, washing away the false amber of the docks until only the raw, un-sculpted baseline of Kim Jin-Young remained.
On the rough pine table beside the wash-vat, three certified credsticks lay beside an empty brass burner.
The ledger was an operational disaster. Mr. Fa’s panicked transfer had cleared at seven thousand nuyen, but the shadows in Hong Kong demanded their toll in blood and silver. One thousand had vanished into the coat pocket of a Port Authority watch commander at the outer gate; crossroad silver pressed into a nervous palm to ensure the security subroutines logging their vehicle were purged before CorpSec arrived. Another two thousand had gone directly to the elderly herbalist upstairs for clean saline, sulfur burn pastes, sterile shears, and dry woolen blankets. Factoring in transit chits and ferry bribes to move their human cargo south of the cordon, the contract had closed at a net financial loss.
Mitsuhama’s actuarial routines, hardwired into his early education, categorized the deficit as an irrecoverable failure of resource management. Yet looking at the red balances on his commlink slate, his pulse was a slow, unwavering core. The nuyen was simply spent tallow, burned to keep the wolves off the threshold.
Across the stone floor, huddled against the warmth of the hot-water pipes, sat seven street kids and runaways pulled from the belly of shipping container CT4.
They were silent, wrapped in coarse grey wool, their small frames shivering with the lingering static aftershocks of the dockland assault. The storm had breached the perimeter, but an air spirit possessed no concept of thermal conductivity. When the lightning had struck the corrugated alloy of the holding pens, the current had surged through the structural ribs, superheating the interior metal and showering the captives in white-hot molten slag.
A fifteen-year-old girl near the boiler hissed in pain, clutching a forearm where charred cotton had fused directly into blistered, weeping skin.
Velvet stood up from the crate. His legs were stiff from the cartilage reset, but the tremors in his hands were a lingering reflex of corporate adrenaline that needed to be cleared. In Mitsuhama’s idol facilities, coaxing the spirits had been drilled as a cold, biomechanical protocol: align the mental vectors, force the mana through neural pathways like high-voltage current, and bind the external entity as a disposable battery to bear the feedback.
He stepped to the center of the flagstones, lowered his chin, and emptied the vessel. He cleared the floor of his own ego, relaxing the tension in his diaphragm and inviting the spirits across the threshold.
The air in the cellar shifted. The caustic tang of vinegar and zinc softened, replaced by an ancient warmth carrying the dry scent of wild cedar drying over an autumn hearth. For once there was no icy, burning back-voltage of corporate spellcraft; it settled across his collarbones with the comforting weight of a heavy wool blanket. His posture shifted reflexively, his breathing deepening as an unhurried, ancestral stillness anchored his frame.
The spiritual touch moved across his skin in a soft, unhurried invitation. Velvet released his hold on his cosmetic spell-work, allowing the spirit to take hold. Beneath the skin, the metahuman geometry yielded. The tapered cartilage of his ears softened and drew inward, rounding into plain human lobes, while the obsidian depth of his Daleketnon irises washed into a warm, everyday tea-brown. Her ribcage pulled inward, bringing the shoulders into a gentle curve, settling into the frame of an ordinary human woman. Her skin took on the dry, warm comfort of unglazed earthenware, radiating a subtle stillness that pushed back the cellar’s chill. The calculating lines of his face yielded, the jawline tapering and cheekbones rounding into the quiet, unadorned composure of an herbalist.
Velvet knelt on the cold stone before the injured girl. When her hands reached out, the tremors were gone. Her fingers moved with an ancient, rhythmic economy she had never studied in corporate training. With a pair of dull brass shears, she cut away the blackened sleeve, her touch so light and steady that the girl’s sharp gasps slowed to quiet whimpers. She dipped a clean linen cloth into a basin of cold herbal tea and boiled saline, cleansing the soot and metal flakes from the raw tissue.
The spirit investing her turned her unearthly presence inward, dampening the active glare of her aura until it became a deep, sedative pool. The room’s ambient anxiety began to unwind. Across the flagstones, the other children stopped their restless shifting, their rapid heart rates slowing in response to the quiet, immovable peace radiating from the kneeling figure.
With unhurried precision, Velvet applied thick coats of cooling camphor salve across the burns, smoothing strips of unbleached cotton over the wounds. When she tied the finishing knots at the wrist, her fingers moved in a distinct, looping braid. It was an old method of untying tension and binding trauma that owed nothing to modern plaster casts.
She moved to the next child, an underfed boy nursing a dislocated shoulder suffered when the container doors were blown inward. Velvet placed one warm palm flat against the boy’s sternum, letting the ancestral weight transfer through the touch to ground the child’s panic. With a single, fluid traction of her other hand against the wrist, the joint slipped back into its socket with a soft, clean pop. The boy flinched, blinked through tears, and then let his head fall forward against Velvet’s shoulder, exhausted beyond fear.
In the corner of the ceiling, a grease-stained trid monitor flickered to life, its audio feed turned low against the hum of the boiler.
The Hong Kong news feed displayed sweeping aerial footage of the Kwai Chung container terminal. Emergency strobes from dozens of Port Authority cruisers painted the gantry cranes in flashing blue, while heavy corporate drones hovered over the charred, twisted wreckage of lot CT4. A crisp, polished anchor praised the swift intervention of local authorities in breaking up a syndicate human trafficking ring, cutting briefly to an interview excerpt authored by Fa Ren, the journalism student whose university thesis had broken the story wide open. On screen, Fa Ren stood outside her father’s apartment, exhausted but resolute, speaking of accountability and corporate negligence with fierce, articulate clarity.
Velvet kept her hands steady on the gauze. She tied the final bandage, smoothed the wool blanket over the boy’s shoulders, and stepped back. The ancestral presence receded like a slow, warming tide, leaving her muscles sore but her center clear. All seven children were asleep, their breathing rhythmic and deep against the low hiss of the copper vats.
She walked to the narrow wooden stairs leading up to the street. She pulled on a plain, dark windbreaker borrowed from the apothecary’s drying rack and zipped it to her throat. She had no active face in this sprawl, no remaining corporate identification, and barely enough nuyen to buy passage on the morning ferry.
She paused at the final landing where a full-length mirror lay against the wall. Her eyes took in the form of the delicate, soft featured young woman looking back at her, her short, dark hair plastered to her forehead by sweat and steam from the boiling vats. A small shadow creased her brow as she stared at the reflection, the corners of her mouth turning downward in a barely perceptible frown. With a quiet sigh, she reached up and gently touched her cheek, her expression unreadable as she took in the changes wrought by the spirits, before turning away and ascending the stairs to the street.
“What is your name?” Velvet mused at her reflection. Unexpectedly, her mouth moved on its own accord. Her lips formed the shape of syllables: Kang Anning.
Pushing open the heavy alley door, Velvet stepped out into the damp, sulfur-tinted dawn of Kowloon. Across Victoria Harbour, the emerald spire of the Wuxing Skytower caught the first pale light of morning, cold and untouchable above the mist. Velvet pulled her hood low against the harbor drizzle, turned her back on the tower, and walked down into the crowded streets with clean hands, an empty ledger, and an unburdened soul.

Rather than collapsing into psychosis, these disparate fragments braid into a higher-order, hyper-evolved composite consciousness capable of autonomous agency.

Mitsuhama Applied Technologies engineered Jin-Young’s bio-sculpting, voice modulation, and infiltration covers as disposable, exploitative tools.

2. Comparative Metaphysical & Theological Taxonomy

A. Mahayana & Tantric Vajrayana Buddhism








Concept
Traditional Definition
Manifestation in Velvet’s Arc




Anattā (Non-Self) (무아 / 無我)
The truth that phenomena lack an immutable, independent “I” (ātman); selfhood is an impermanent aggregate (skandhas).
Corporate conditioning treated identity erasure as spiritual murder. Under Buddhist insight, having no static core is not a void of deficiency, but ultimate liberation: because Velvet is empty, he has boundless capacity to inhabit form.


Śūnyatā (Emptiness) (공 / 空)
Reality is empty of inherent, fixed existence; all phenomena arise interdependently as pure potential.
Emptiness is not nothingness—it is the quiet, unconditioned canvas of the un-sculpted baseline upon which any human life can be authentically painted.


Upāya-kauśalya (Skillful Means) (방편 / 方便)
The practice of enlightened beings adopting provisional guises and methods tailored to liberate beings and alleviate suffering.
Personas (Lee Ji-yoo, Tanaka Ryo, Mei Jing, Zhang Wei) cease to be cynical corporate lies; they become compassionate, deliberate instruments of protection, survival, and justice.


Nirmāṇakāya (Transformation Body) (변화신 / 變化身)
The manifest physical emanation body projected by a Bodhisattva into the material realm.
Avalokiteśvara (Gwan-eum / Kannon) projects 33 distinct manifest forms (courtesan, beggar, general, healer) to meet suffering where it lives. Velvet’s operational covers function as literal nirmāṇakāya.


Indra’s Jewel Net (인드라망 / 因陀羅網)
An infinite cosmic matrix where each jewel’s facet reflects every other jewel in the universe.
Every persona Velvet embodies reflects the memories and virtues of all other lives, weaving a holographic web of intersubjective empathy.




Tantric Vajrayana Deity Yoga (Utpattikrama & Sampannakrama)
In Tibetan Buddhist tantra, the practitioner practices two reciprocal stages of transformation:

Generation Stage (Utpattikrama): The practitioner dissolves ordinary ego-attachment into the void (Śūnyatā), then consciously manifests the divine form of the Yidam—complete with distinct garments, posture, acoustic resonance, and spiritual attributes. Velvet’s somatic shifting via Cosmetic Control operates as a conscious Utpattikrama, constructing physical bone alignment, vocal cadence, and aura without egoic clinging.
Completion Stage (Sampannakrama): Upon concluding the rite, the form is mindfully dissolved back into luminous stillness. Velvet utilizes Sampannakrama at the end of runs to dissolve mission personas back into the quiet baseline, preventing psychological fragmentation or attachment to a false face.

Early bio-sculpting trauma under Mitsuhama: the visceral agony of cartilage resets, burning DNA re-keying, and identity dissociation. The horror of being an overwritten tool.

Velvet’s transition from resisting manufactured covers to consciously hosting them with reverence, discipline, and ritual care.

An accomplished Mudang capable of hosting, understanding, and speaking for ten thousand divine and ancestral spirits.
Velvet becomes the Mansin of his own lived lives. Past personas form an internal ancestral conclave whose collective wisdom and grief are honored.

In classical Gnosticism, humanity’s divine spark (Pneuma) is trapped by Archons headed by the Demiurge. The Archons fabricate the Anti-mimon Pneuma (Counterfeit Spirit)—a conditioned false ego designed to compel obedience through fear and desire.
Mitsuhama’s engineered pop idol persona was a literal Anti-mimon Pneuma. Velvet’s awakening is Gnosis: recognizing the corporate idol as a counterfeit shell, liberating the true Pneuma beneath, and turning corporate techniques back against the megacorporate Demiurge.

Paul Ricoeur (Oneself as Another / Soi-même comme un autre):

Ricoeur distinguishes between Idem-identity (numerical and physical sameness over time) and Ipse-identity (narrative selfhood, fidelity, and ethical promise-keeping).

Keats defined the highest artistic consciousness as one capable of “being in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason.” The Chameleon Poet possesses no fixed self because it continually inhabits the lives and forms of others.
